newsitem.title: USA: US capital securities escape Archer's tax axe - PSA.
newsitem.headline: US capital securities escape Archer's tax axe - PSA.

text.p: Several debt securities favored by Wall Street escaped the axe in tax legislation introduced on Capitol Hill on Monday, PSA The Bond Market Trade Association executive vice president Micah Green said.

In his tax plan, U.S. House Ways and Means Committee Chairman Bill Archer did not include a proposal that would have eliminated the tax deductibility of capital securities with maturities longer than 15 years.
He also excluded similar proposals for bonds with maturities longer than 40 years and for convertible original issue discount bonds.
All three proposals were originally offered in President Clinton's tax plan as a means to raise additional revenue to help balance the U.S. federal budget.

"This is significant," said Green. "(Archer's proposal) serves as a framework for debate in the Ways and Means committee on the tax bill. It sets a tone that these revenue items may not be looked upon favorably by the chairman."
Green added that because of the technical nature of the tax proposals it would be difficult for them to be considered in the upcoming debate in the committee.
But Green said that the current situation may not be final.
He noted that there was still a chance that Senate Finance Committee Chairman William Roth may include the proposals in his own tax plan, which could be released as early as next week.

Green said that even if the Senate tax panel does not adopt them, the proposals could be added while the tax bill is being considered on the floor of the Senate, where rules for debate are more liberal.
"We are gratified that Chairman Archer has not included the (proposals) in his package, but we are also very realistic that this is only the first step of the process," Green said.
Banks and corporations have issued over $30 billion in capital securities, also known as trust preferred stock in recent years.
Under current tax law, issuers of capital securities may deduct dividend payments, similar to debt securities, while still receiving certain benefits associated with equity financing.
Bonds with maturities longer than 40-years, such as 100-year bonds or "century bonds," have become popular in recent years, particularly as U.S. interest rates have fallen.
The Clinton Adminstration hoped to raise approximately $1 billion by eliminating the tax-advantaged status of these securities, tax experts said.

"I think people realize that these instruments are being utilized very responsibly to reduce the cost of capital," said Green. "It seems very counterproductive to eliminate them by virtue of some arbitrary ruling."
